_**User (2026-06-05 08:09:48Z)**_

bei erstem testen der Smart-Häufige-Updates Funktion in echter Live Umgebung ist aufgefallen dass sich die Funktion erst bei der übernächsten Standortaktualisierung einschaltet und nicht gleich mit der ersten die verfügbar wird. Kann das sein? Weiterhin scheinen nicht wirklich alle Location Updates dann verwertet zu werden (ist nur ein Gefühl, trotz dann selbständig aktiviertem Smart-Häufige-Updates kommen relativ wenig updates - könnte das an der 25m Distanz-Regel liegen? Analysiere und brainstorme hier im chat mit mir problem-möglichkeiten sowie lösungswege

     1	# Smart Frequent Background Updates
     2	
     3	Date: 2026-06-04
     4	
     5	## Summary
     6	
     7	Miataru 3.2 changes frequent background tracking from one flat manual toggle into a two-stage model:
     8	
     9	- Stage 1, Smart frequent updates, is off by default.
    10	- Stage 2, manual frequent background updates, becomes available after Stage 1 is enabled and overrides Smart behavior completely.
    11	
    12	Smart frequent updates keep the battery-saving standard background mode, backed by significant-change monitoring, as the normal state. When a significant-change update shows movement above the configured speed threshold, Smart temporarily starts frequent background updates. Frequent runtime is stopped again when the shared inactivity window expires because no location update arrived or because no relevant movement over the configured frequent distance filter was observed.
    13	
    14	## User-Facing Behavior
    15	
    16	Smart frequent settings live in Advanced Options under the background location section:
    17	
    18	- Smart frequent updates: default off.
    19	- Speed threshold: 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, or 30 km/h; default 10 km/h.
    20	- Speed detection: Hybrid or GPS-only; default Hybrid.
    21	- Smart inactivity window: 5, 10, 15, or 30 minutes; default 10 minutes.
    22	- Smart frequent mode-change notifications: default off.
    23	
    24	Hybrid speed detection uses valid `CLLocation.speed` first. If GPS speed is not valid, it derives speed from distance and elapsed time between usable location samples. GPS-only mode ignores derived speed and only uses `CLLocation.speed`. Smart activation rejects implausible activation speeds above 200 km/h so startup/reset GPS spikes do not switch frequent runtime on.
    25	
    26	The inactivity window is shared by both Smart stop conditions:
    27	
    28	- no location update within the selected window;
    29	- no movement over the frequent distance filter within the selected window.
    30	
    31	Manual frequent background updates keep the existing distance, duration, delivery delay, visitor-check interval, reminder/expiration notifications, and low-battery auto-disable behavior. Smart frequent runtime uses the same frequent distance, delivery-delay, and visitor-check interval policies. Manual mode ignores Smart activation and inactivity criteria while it is enabled.
    32	
    33	## Migration
    34	
    35	Existing installs with manual frequent background updates enabled are preserved. During migration, Miataru enables the Smart prerequisite and leaves manual frequent mode enabled, so the effective behavior remains manual frequent tracking after the update.
    36	
    37	There is also startup normalization for externally changed settings: if manual frequent mode is enabled through the iOS Settings.bundle while the Smart prerequisite is off, the app re-enables the Smart prerequisite on load.
    38	
    39	## Runtime Implementation
    40	
    41	`LocationManager` keeps Smart runtime state in memory only. After relaunch, Smart starts in the waiting state. The first background location in a fresh process seeds Smart's speed/movement reference and cannot activate frequent runtime by itself; a later qualifying significant-change update can activate Smart once movement is measured against that in-process reference.
    42	
    43	The effective frequent background state is:
    44	
    45	```text
    46	manual frequent enabled OR (Smart enabled AND Smart runtime active)
    47	```
    48	
    49	Smart activation only happens from primary significant-change callbacks while the app is not active. Smart runtime does not activate from foreground/live updates or from secondary frequent-manager callbacks.
    50	
    51	Battery auto-disable acts on the effective frequent state. For manual frequent mode it turns off the manual preference; for Smart frequent runtime it only stops the Smart runtime and leaves the user's Smart preference intact.
    52	
    53	## Notifications
    54	
    55	`FrequentBackgroundTrackingReminderService` now owns four frequent-background notification families:
    56	
    57	- 24-hour reminder for never-expiring manual frequent mode;
    58	- one-shot expiration notification for finite manual frequent durations;
    59	- low-battery auto-disable notification;
    60	- optional Smart frequent mode-change notifications.
    61	
    62	Smart mode-change notifications are sent only when enabled by the user. Enabling them requests notification permission first; denied permission leaves the setting off and the UI offers a shortcut to the app's system settings. They fire when Smart itself activates frequent runtime after detected movement or deactivates frequent runtime because the inactivity window elapsed. _**Agent (gpt-5.5 2026-06-05 08:13:49Z)**_

Ja, das kann sehr gut sein. Nach Code-Lage ist es sogar teilweise erwartetes Verhalten: Smart hat nur eine In-Memory-Referenz. Nach Cold Start/Location-Launch kann die erste Background-Location deshalb nur die Referenz setzen; aktivieren kann erst eine spätere Location, weil `canActivateSmartFrequentBackgroundUpdates` eine vorherige Location verlangt. Siehe [LocationManager.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/LocationManagers/LocationManager.swift:1452) und die Doku in [smart-frequent-background-updates-2026-06-04.md](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/documentation/smart-frequent-background-updates-2026-06-04.md:41).

Wichtig: Es kann zusätzlich nur so aussehen, als schalte Smart erst beim nächsten Tick, weil der Update-Modus im `didUpdateLocations` vor der Smart-Umschaltung gezählt wird. Die Aktivierungs-Location wird also noch als `significantChange` gezählt, Smart-Frequent sieht man im Zähler erst beim nächsten Callback. Siehe [LocationManager.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/LocationManagers/LocationManager.swift:2027).

Zur zweiten Beobachtung: Ja, die 25m-Regel kann daran beteiligt sein, aber sie ist nicht die einzige Drossel. Der Pfad hat mehrere Filter:

- `didUpdateLocations` verwertet aktuell nur `locations.last`. Wenn iOS mehrere Locations in einem Callback bündelt, werden frühere Punkte ignoriert.
- Der Frequent-Manager nutzt `distanceFilter` 25/50/100m. Die erlaubten Werte stehen in [SettingsConfiguration.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/SettingsManagers/App%20Settings/SettingsConfiguration.swift:219).
- Danach kommt zusätzlich die App-eigene Sensitivität: default 5m/5m, Batteriesparen 25m/20m, Minimal 50m/40m. Nicht angenommene Updates werden nicht gecached/hochgeladen.
- Smart nutzt denselben Frequent-Distanzfilter auch als “relevante Bewegung” für die Inaktivitätslogik. Wenn innerhalb des Fensters keine Bewegung über z.B. 25m erkannt wird, kann Smart wieder abschalten.
- Falls “Auslieferung” nicht auf sofort steht, queued der Coordinator Background-Updates absichtlich bis zum gewählten Fenster. Siehe [LocationUpdateDeliveryCoordinator.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/Networking/LocationUpdateDeliveryCoordinator.swift:118).

Meine wahrscheinlichsten Problemquellen wären daher:

1. **By-design, aber UX-unintuitiv:** erste reale Background-Location nach Neustart seeded nur.
2. **Diagnose-Artefakt:** Aktivierungs-Update wird noch als Standard gezählt.
3. **Echte Unterverwertung:** `locations.last` statt alle Locations aus dem Callback.
4. **Doppelte Distanzfilterung:** iOS-25m plus App-Sensitivität plus Smart-Relevant-Movement.
5. **Sparse Significant-Change vor Aktivierung:** Smart wartet in einem Modus, der von iOS naturgemäß selten feuert.

Lösungswege, die ich sinnvoll finde:

- **Diagnose zuerst:** Raw callbacks, `locations.count`, accepted/ignored reason, Smart rejection reason, upload/queued/deduped zählen. Das würde sofort zeigen, ob iOS wenig liefert oder Miataru viel wegfiltert.
- **Schneller aktivieren:** Smart-Referenz aus `latestRawLocation/currentLocation` oder persistentem letztem Standort vorseeded verwenden; alternativ gültige `CLLocation.speed` auch ohne vorherige Referenz aktivieren lassen.
- **Mehr Updates verwerten:** In Frequent-Mode die App-Sensitivität lockern oder umgehen, weil iOS bereits per `distanceFilter` drosselt.
- **Batch-Handling verbessern:** `didUpdateLocations` chronologisch über alle Locations laufen lassen, zumindest für Smart-Erkennung und optional für Upload/History.

Für Live-Test würde ich temporär setzen: Smart-Schwelle 2 km/h, Distanz 25m, Inaktivität 30min, Auslieferung sofort, Sensitivität “Standard” oder “Sehr empfindlich”, Akku über Auto-Disable-Schwelle. Dann sieht man klarer, ob der Engpass CoreLocation oder unsere Filterlogik ist.

PLEASE IMPLEMENT THIS PLAN:
# Smart-Frequent Updatewertung Härtung

## Summary
- Der separate Frequent-/Smart-Bewegungsschwellen-Regler bleibt erhalten.
- Die Bewegungsschwelle wird um `10m` und `5m` erweitert, zusätzlich zu `25m`, `50m`, `100m`.
- Smart kann beim ersten Background-Update nach Relaunch aktivieren, wenn ein persistenter, frischer Standort-Seed vorhanden ist.
- `didUpdateLocations` verarbeitet künftig alle verwertbaren Locations eines Callbacks chronologisch statt nur `locations.last`.

## Key Changes
- **Bewegungsschwelle erweitern:** `FrequentBackgroundLocationDistanceFilter` erlaubt künftig `[100, 50, 25, 10, 5]`; UI und Settings.bundle zeigen die neuen Optionen.
- **Bestehende Semantik behalten:** Die Bewegungsschwelle bleibt zuständig für den Frequent-`distanceFilter` und Smart-“relevante Bewegung”. Die appweite Standort-Sensitivität bleibt weiterhin nur die separate Akzeptanzlogik für Cache/Upload.
- **Persistenter Smart-Seed:** Den letzten validen Raw-Standort persistieren. Beim Restore/Location-Launch als `smartFrequentBackgroundSpeedReferenceLocation` verwenden, aber nur wenn der Timestamp frisch genug ist und daraus keine implausible Geschwindigkeit entsteht.
- **Batch-Verarbeitung:** `didUpdateLocations` in eine Schleife über chronologisch sortierte Locations refactoren. Jede verwertbare Location aktualisiert Raw-State, Smart-State, Cache und Upload-Queue; Tracking-Modus wird pro Callback nur einmal am Ende neu angewendet.
- **Upload-Reihenfolge:** Mehrere akzeptierte Locations aus einem Batch werden sequenziell an den `LocationUpdateDeliveryCoordinator` übergeben, damit History/Server-Updates zeitlich korrekt bleiben und Deduping weiterhin greift.
- **Diagnose korrigieren:** Mode-Zähler nach Smart-State-Verarbeitung berechnen, damit die Aktivierungs-Location nicht mehr als reiner Significant-Change-Tick wirkt.

## Akku-Implikation
- `5m` und `10m` können im Smart-/Manual-Frequent-Modus deutlich mehr CoreLocation-Callbacks, Uploads und Inaktivitäts-Timer-Resets auslösen.
- Standard-Smart-Waiting bleibt weiterhin sparsam, weil dort significant-change monitoring aktiv bleibt.
- Bestehende Schutzmechanismen bleiben wichtig: Inactivity Window, Low-Battery-Auto-Disable, Delivery-Batching und Outbox.

## Test Plan
- Unit-Tests für Bewegungsschwellen-Normalisierung: `5`, `10`, `25`, `50`, `100` gültig; ungültige Werte fallen auf Default zurück.
- Settings-Tests: UI-/Settings.bundle-Optionen enthalten `5m` und `10m`; Defaults bleiben kompatibel.
- Smart-Seed-Tests: frischer Seed aktiviert beim ersten Background-Update; stale/implausible Seeds werden ignoriert.
- Batch-Tests: mehrere Locations in einem Callback werden chronologisch verarbeitet, verwertbare Punkte hochgeladen, invalid/duplicate Punkte übersprungen.
- Regression: Manual-Frequent-Override, Battery-Auto-Disable, Outbox, Delivery-Delay und Smart-Inactivity bleiben unverändert funktionsfähig.

## Assumptions
- Der bisherige Default `100m` bleibt bestehen.
- Horizontal-Accuracy-spezifische Smart-Logik bleibt ausdrücklich außerhalb dieses Plans.
- Appweite Sensitivität und Frequent-Bewegungsschwelle bleiben vorerst getrennte Einstellungen.

+                let lhsTimestamp = lhs.element.timestamp
+                let rhsTimestamp = rhs.element.timestamp
+                if lhsTimestamp == rhsTimestamp {

+                }
+                return lhsTimestamp < rhsTimestamp
+            }

+            return false
+        }
+
+        let age = now.timeIntervalSince(seedTimestamp)

+

+        let accuracyImprovement = previousLocation.horizontalAccuracy - location.horizontalAccuracy
+        if distance >= minimumDistance {
+            debugLog("[LocationManager] Location update accepted: distance (\(distance)m) >= minimum (\(minimumDistance)m)")
+            return true
+        }
+        if accuracyImprovement >= significantAccuracyImprovement {
+            debugLog("[LocationManager] Location update accepted: accuracy improved by (\(accuracyImprovement)m) >= minimum (\(significantAccuracyImprovement)m)")

        guard isTracking else { return .stopped }

            return .active

            return .background
        }
    }

    static func batteryPercent(from batteryLevel: Float) -> Int? {

    static func processableLocationUpdates(from locations: [CLLocation]) -> [CLLocation] {
        locations

                return coordinate.latitude.isFinite &&
                coordinate.longitude.isFinite &&
                CLLocationCoordinate2DIsValid(coordinate) &&
                location.timestamp.timeIntervalSince1970.isFinite
            }
            .sorted { lhs, rhs in
                let lhsTimestamp = lhs.element.timestamp
                let rhsTimestamp = rhs.element.timestamp
                if lhsTimestamp == rhsTimestamp {
                    return lhs.offset < rhs.offset
                }
                return lhsTimestamp < rhsTimestamp
            }
            .map(\.element)
    }

        }

    private func apply(_ mode: TrackingMode) {

        switch mode {
        case .stopped:
            stopAllLocationServices()
        case .foregroundHighAccuracy:
            startHighAccuracyUpdates()
        case .backgroundSignificantChange:
            startSignificantChangeMonitoring()
        case .backgroundFrequent(let distanceFilter, let desiredAccuracy):

                desiredAccuracy: desiredAccuracy
            )

        }

    private func blendedHeading(compass: Double, course: Double?, speed: Double?) -> Double {
        let normalizedCompass = normalizedHeading(compass)
        guard let course, course >= 0, let speed, speed >= headingMinSpeedThreshold else {
            return normalizedCompass
        }
        let normalizedCourse = normalizedHeading(course)
        let weight = min(max(speed / 4.0, 0.0), 1.0)
        let delta = normalizedCourse - normalizedCompass
        let wrappedDelta: Double = {
            if delta > 180 { return delta - 360 }
            if delta < -180 { return delta + 360 }
            return delta
        }()
        return normalizedHeading(normalizedCompass + wrappedDelta * weight)
    }

    private func maybeResetBackgroundMetricsIfNeeded(now: Date = Date()) {
        let lastReset = userDefaults.object(forKey: backgroundMetricsLastResetKey) as? Date
        guard let lastReset else {
            userDefaults.set(now, forKey: backgroundMetricsLastResetKey)

        maybeResetBackgroundMetricsIfNeeded(now: now)
        locationUpdateModeCounts.increment(mode)
        if mode != .foregroundLive {
            lastBackgroundUpdate = now
            backgroundUpdateCount = locationUpdateModeCounts.backgroundTotal
            userDefaults.set(backgroundUpdateCount, forKey: backgroundUpdateCountKey)
            userDefaults.set(now, forKey: lastBackgroundUpdateKey)
        }
        persistLocationUpdateModeCounts()
    }

        userDefaults.set(locationUpdateModeCounts.smartFrequent, forKey: smartFrequentUpdateCountKey)

PY

    private static func unknownVisitorVisitDate(from userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any]) -> Date? {
        let rawValue = userInfo[UnknownVisitorAlertService.notificationVisitTimestampUserInfoKey]
        let timestampMs: Int64?

        if let value = rawValue as? Int64 {
            timestampMs = value
        } else if let value = rawValue as? Int {
            timestampMs = Int64(value)
        } else if let value = rawValue as? NSNumber {
            timestampMs = value.int64Value
        } else if let value = rawValue as? String {
            timestampMs = Int64(value)
        } else {
            timestampMs = nil
        }

        guard let timestampMs else { return nil }
        return Date(timeIntervalSince1970: Double(timestampMs) / 1_000.0)
    }

_**Agent (gpt-5.5 2026-06-05 09:08:50Z)**_

Kurz: Unsere Änderungen sollten das Reboot/App-Restart-Verhalten für Significant-Change nicht verschlechtern. Der Pfad bleibt erhalten.

Was passiert aktuell:

- Bei normalem App-Start ruft [miataruApp.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/miataruApp.swift:270) `LocationManager.shared.restoreTrackingAfterLaunch(reason: "app launch")`, wenn `trackAndReportLocation` aktiv ist.
- Bei einem iOS-Location-Relaunch, also `UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey.location`, ruft der `AppDelegate` bereits in `willFinishLaunching`/`didFinishLaunching` `restoreTrackingAfterLaunch(reason: "location launch", applicationStateContext: .forceBackground)` auf.
- Im Restore setzt [LocationManager.swift](/Users/bietiekay/code/miataru-ios-app/miataru/miataru/LocationManagers/LocationManager.swift:1099) `isTracking = true` und ruft `applyTrackingMode(...)`.
- `applyTrackingMode` hält den Significant-Change-Recovery-Anchor, wenn Tracking aktiv ist, `authorizedAlways` vorliegt und kein DeviceKey-Auth-Block aktiv ist.
- `Info.plist` enthält `UIBackgroundModes = location`, also die notwendige Background-Location-Capability.

Die neue Smart-Seed-/Batch-Änderung greift erst nach einem Location-Callback. Sie entfernt oder ersetzt den Significant-Change-Anchor nicht. Im Frequent-Modus wird der Primary-Manager weiterhin für Significant-Change registriert, während Frequent-Updates über den zweiten Manager laufen.

Die echten Bedingungen bleiben also:

- `trackAndReportLocation == true`
- Standortberechtigung ist `Always`
- App wurde nicht durch DeviceKey-Auth blockiert
- iOS hat die App nicht durch Nutzer-Force-Quit in den Zustand gebracht, in dem Background-Relaunches bis zum manuellen Start unterdrückt werden

Nach normalem App-Restart oder Device-Reboot sollte iOS bei einem späteren Significant-Location-Event die App wieder starten und der Restore-Pfad sollte das Monitoring wieder herstellen. Garantie im Sinne von “sofort nach Reboot aktiv ohne Event” gibt es bei Significant-Change nicht; der Trigger ist ein signifikantes Standortereignis.

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.5 2026-06-05 09:11:11Z)**_

Kurz: Nein, nicht zuverlässig zum Zeitpunkt des Force-Quit.

Wenn der Nutzer die App im App-Switcher “wegwischt”, bekommt die App normalerweise keinen verlässlichen Callback mehr, in dem sie noch sagen könnte: “Aha, Force-Quit, jetzt Notification senden.” Apple dokumentiert auch, dass `applicationWillTerminate` bei Apps mit Background-Ausführung im normalen Quit-/Background-Fall im Allgemeinen nicht aufgerufen wird. Eine Notification müsste also vorher geplant worden sein, nicht erst beim Force-Quit. Quellen: [applicationWillTerminate](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiapplicationdelegate/1623111-applicationwillterminate), [UIApplicationLaunchOptionsLocationKey](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiapplicationlaunchoptionslocationkey), [Core Location Location Awareness Guide](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/UserExperience/Conceptual/LocationAwarenessPG/CoreLocation/CoreLocation.html).

Was möglich wäre:

1. **In-App-/Settings-Warnung**
   Klarer Hinweis bei aktivem Background-Tracking: “Wenn du Miataru aus dem App-Switcher beendest, werden Standortupdates bis zum manuellen Start nicht fortgesetzt.”

2. **Einmalige Educational Notification**
   Beim Aktivieren von Background-Tracking oder beim ersten Wechsel in den Hintergrund eine lokale Notification planen: “Nicht aus dem App-Switcher beenden, wenn Standortupdates weiterlaufen sollen.”  
   Nachteil: Sie erkennt keinen tatsächlichen Force-Quit, sondern ist nur präventiv.

3. **Heuristik beim nächsten manuellen Start**
   Beim nächsten Start prüfen: Tracking war aktiv, letzter Standort ist alt, Launch war kein `.location`-Launch. Dann In-App-Hinweis anzeigen: “Möglicherweise wurden Updates durch Force-Quit oder iOS/Settings unterbrochen.”  
   Das ist aber rückblickend und nicht beweisbar.

4. **Statuskarte in den Einstellungen**
   Zeigen: “Background-Tracking aktiv”, “Significant-Change-Restore bereit”, “Letztes Background-Update vor X”, plus Warnung bei sehr altem Update.

Für Miataru würde ich am ehesten Option 1 + 4 machen, eventuell mit einer einmaligen, sehr zurückhaltenden Educational Notification. Eine echte “Force-Quit erkannt, jetzt warnen”-Notification geht mit öffentlichen iOS-APIs nicht zuverlässig.

# Frequent Background Session Hardening

Date: 2026-05-29

## Summary

Real-device testing showed that reboot-safe significant-change tracking was stable, but frequent background updates could degrade into short update bursts separated by significant-change wakeups. The frequent update stream resumed briefly after the primary significant-change manager delivered an event, then paused again.

This follow-up keeps the primary `CLLocationManager` as the durable significant-change reboot anchor and keeps frequent standard updates on the secondary manager, but adds explicit runtime support for live frequent background tracking.

## Implementation

- Active `Always`-authorized tracking now holds an `Always` `CLServiceSession`, including standard significant-change mode.
- Frequent background mode additionally holds a `CLBackgroundActivitySession` while the mode is active.
- The Always service session is stopped when tracking is stopped, authorization is lost, or DeviceKey authentication blocks uploads. The frequent background activity session is also stopped when frequent mode is disabled, expires, or is disabled for low battery.
- A primary significant-change callback can reassert frequent standard updates only if frequent standard updates were already active in the current process. This avoids restoring frequent mode aggressively after a cold reboot location wakeup.
- In standard significant-change mode, a background primary callback reasserts significant-change monitoring again. This keeps the post-reboot path from relying only on launch-time reconstruction after the first delivered location.
- The secondary frequent manager is stopped more defensively when frequent mode is inactive: standard updates and significant-change monitoring are stopped, background updates are disabled, automatic pausing is restored, and the delegate is detached.
- If a stale secondary callback arrives just after frequent mode was stopped, the first valid location can still flow through the normal deduped upload path. Repeated stale callbacks are suppressed after cleanup.

## Expected Behavior

- Standard significant-change tracking remains the reboot/system-termination recovery path.
- Frequent mode should produce continuous background standard location updates while the app is alive and the mode is active.
- Disabling or expiring frequent mode falls back to significant-change tracking without continuing to receive uploads from the secondary frequent manager.
- After a reboot while frequent mode is enabled, Miataru still resumes via significant-change tracking first; saved frequent mode resumes when the app is started normally.

## Validation

- Real-device testing by the user confirmed the final behavior.
- `xcodebuild -quiet -project miataru/miataru.xcodeproj -scheme miataru -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,id=73874736-DD77-4211-B78B-A50B1A6FB2B9' -only-testing:miataruTests/SettingsConfigurationTests test`
- `xcodebuild -quiet -project miataru/miataru.xcodeproj -scheme miataru -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' build`
- `git diff --check`
```

# Background Location Reboot Hardening

Date: 2026-05-27

## Summary

Real-device testing showed that the first reboot-safe recovery-anchor implementation was still not sufficient: after rebooting an iPhone while frequent background updates were active, Miataru could fail to resume both frequent updates and significant-change updates until the app was opened manually.

This follow-up keeps the recovery-anchor architecture, but hardens the launch and delivery edges that matter after iOS starts the app in the background for location.

## Problem

The app had two fragile points:

- Location recovery was handled in `didFinishLaunchingWithOptions`, after some app bootstrap work had already started. For a location-triggered background launch, the app should restore tracking as early as possible.
- A received background location could start an async server upload without explicit background-task protection. If iOS suspended the app quickly after a reboot/location relaunch, the location might be observed locally but not delivered to the server.

The resolver also allowed `authorizedWhenInUse` to resolve to background tracking. That is not a durable state for reboot recovery, because iOS background relaunch for location requires the app to have sufficient background-capable authorization.

## Implementation

- `AppDelegate` now restores tracking from `application(_:willFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` when the launch options contain `UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey.location`.
- The same recovery check remains in `didFinishLaunchingWithOptions`, guarded by a single-launch dedupe flag.
- `LocationManager` wraps non-foreground location uploads in a short `UIApplication.beginBackgroundTask` token and ends it when the async upload path completes.
- `LocationManager.resolvedTrackingMode(...)` now treats `authorizedWhenInUse` as foreground-only. Background tracking, including frequent background mode and significant-change recovery, requires `authorizedAlways`.
- Frequent background mode keeps the dedicated significant-change recovery manager registered while the primary manager runs `startUpdatingLocation()`.

## Expected Behavior

- With tracking enabled, `Always` authorization, no DeviceKey auth block, and no user force-quit, significant-change monitoring remains the reboot/system-termination recovery anchor.
- Frequent background mode still uses standard background location updates for higher cadence while the app is alive in the background.
- If frequent mode expires or is disabled by low battery, the app falls back to standard significant-change tracking instead of stopping all tracking.
- If the app is relaunched by iOS for location after reboot or system termination, tracking is reconstructed before normal app startup continues and the resulting background upload gets protected execution time.

## Remaining iOS Boundaries

- A user force-quit still prevents background relaunch until the user opens the app again.
- `When In Use` authorization is not treated as reboot-capable background tracking.
- Simulator shutdown/restart is not a reliable proof for significant-change relaunch behavior; real-device tests remain required for reboot validation.
- iOS can still defer or coalesce significant-change delivery based on movement, radio state, power policy, and system scheduling.

## Validation

Focused regression tests passed:

```sh
xcodebuild -project miataru/miataru.xcodeproj -scheme miataru -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' -only-testing:miataruTests/SettingsConfigurationTests test
```

The focused suite executed 12 tests with 0 failures.

**Add: `miataru/documentation/smart-frequent-updatewertung-hardening-2026-06-05.md`**

```diff
+# Smart Frequent Update Evaluation Hardening
+
+Date: 2026-06-05
+
+## Summary
+
+Real-environment testing showed two Smart frequent edge cases:
+
+- Smart frequent runtime could activate only on the second usable background update after relaunch because the first update was used to seed the speed reference.
+- A single Core Location callback can contain multiple locations, but the app previously evaluated only the last entry. That could hide usable intermediate samples and make Smart frequent updates feel sparser than the device actually delivered them.
+
+This follow-up keeps the separate frequent/Smart movement threshold setting, avoids adding horizontal-accuracy-specific Smart logic for now, and hardens the existing update path.
+
+## Implementation
+
+- The frequent background movement threshold now accepts `100`, `50`, `25`, `10`, and `5` meters. The default remains `100` meters.
+- The iPhone Advanced Options picker and Settings.bundle movement-threshold picker expose the new 10 m and 5 m options.
+- The compact `5m` and `10m` string-catalog labels are explicitly marked as non-translatable literals with comments, while the explanatory 5 m and 10 m strings are localized across all supported app locales.
+- `LocationManager` persists the last valid raw location as a Smart frequent seed. On app restore or location launch, the seed becomes the Smart speed reference only when it is fresh according to the selected inactivity window.
+- Persisted seeds still flow through the existing plausible-speed guard. Derived activation speeds above the Smart frequent maximum are ignored, preventing unrealistic post-start activation.
+- `didUpdateLocations` now filters invalid coordinates and non-finite timestamps, sorts the remaining locations chronologically, and evaluates each usable sample.
+- Each processed sample updates raw state, Smart state, diagnostics, heading fallback, cache acceptance, and the upload queue. The tracking mode is reapplied only once at the end of the callback.
+- Accepted batch locations are submitted sequentially to `LocationUpdateDeliveryCoordinator`, preserving chronological history/server order while keeping existing deduplication in place.
+
+## Battery Implications
+
+The new 5 m and 10 m thresholds can increase Core Location callbacks, accepted updates, server submissions, and Smart inactivity-timer resets whenever manual frequent mode or Smart frequent runtime is active.
+
+The default Smart waiting mode remains sparse because it continues to use significant-change monitoring until Smart frequent runtime activates. Existing safeguards remain important: inactivity timeout, low-battery auto-disable, delayed delivery batching, retry outbox, and duplicate upload suppression.
+
+## Expected Behavior
+
+- A fresh persisted seed can allow the first post-relaunch background update to activate Smart frequent runtime if the movement and speed threshold are plausible.
+- Stale, future-dated, invalid, or implausible seeds are ignored and cleared.
+- Batched Core Location callbacks no longer discard usable intermediate points merely because a newer point exists in the same callback.
+- The activation location is counted after Smart state processing, so diagnostics can classify it as Smart frequent instead of a plain significant-change tick.
+- App-wide location sensitivity remains separate from the frequent/Smart movement threshold. It still controls cache/upload acceptance, while the movement threshold controls the frequent `distanceFilter` and Smart relevant-movement policy.
+
+## Validation
+
+- `./scripts/test-unit.sh`
+- `git diff --check`
+- `python3 -m json.tool miataru/miataru/Assets/Localizable.xcstrings`
+- `plutil -lint miataru/miataru/SettingsManagers/App\ Settings/Settings.bundle/Root.plist`
+
+The unit run passed 164 tests, including focused coverage for threshold normalization, Settings.bundle parity, persisted Smart frequent seed freshness/implausible-speed rejection, and chronological batch processing.
```
